statement: Each question on a test has 5 choices, scores 5 points if correct and loses nothing if wrong. Sam has 10 questions left and no time. On 6 he can rule out 3 wrong choices; on the other 4 he can rule out nothing. If he guesses on all 10, how many points should he expect on average?

choices.misconception: I thought a guess is as likely to cost points as to earn them, so on average guessing gains nothing.
I gave every guess a 1 in 5 chance, ignoring the choices Sam can rule out.
I only counted the 6 questions where he narrowed it down to two choices and left out the other 4.
I counted every guess as a correct answer.

hints: How many choices are left on each kind of question?
Since a wrong answer costs nothing, each guess is worth its chance of being right times 5 points. Work out that average for each kind of question and add them up.
With two choices left, a guess is worth half of 5 points, 2.5 on average. With all five choices left, it is worth a fifth of 5 points, 1 on average.

solutions.reliable: On the 6 questions with two choices left, each guess is right half the time, worth 5 / 2 = 2.5 points on average, so 6 x 2.5 = 15 points. On the 4 questions with all five choices, each guess is right one time in five, worth 1 point on average, so 4 points. Altogether Sam expects 15 + 4 = 19 points, compared with 0 for leaving them blank. The transferable idea: with no penalty, a guess is never worse than a blank, and ruling out choices makes it worth much more.

whyOnTest: With no penalty for wrong answers, every blank throws away points; this checks that you can value a guess after ruling out choices.
